stem: An invoice service uses Claude to extract fields from varied PDF layouts. Every invoice then needs vendor-master validation before posting to the accounting API. Extraction already meets the quality target; the remaining requirement is that posting be unreachable when validation fails, with little additional model work. Which design best fits?

options.text: Give an agent extraction, validation, and posting tools, and instruct it to invoke them in that order while retaining their results in its conversation.
Use a fixed extraction workflow with a programmatic validation gate; invoke the posting API from application code after that gate passes.
Ask an orchestrator to assign extraction, validation, and posting to specialist workers, then synthesize their reports into an invoice audit record.
Add a second model to review the extracted fields and vendor policy, then let the extraction model decide whether the invoice is ready to post.

explanation: The workflow can accommodate varied input layouts without giving the model control over posting. Anthropic distinguishes predefined workflow paths from agent-directed tool use and describes programmatic gates between prompt-chain steps. Here application code can enforce the known validation prerequisite, while another planning or judging call adds no necessary capability.

distractorNotes.a: An instruction about order leaves the transition under model control. The requirement is an application-enforced gate, not merely an agent that usually follows the sequence.
distractorNotes.c: Specialist delegation can help with unpredictable subtasks, but collecting worker reports does not establish the required validation gate before posting.
distractorNotes.d: A model review can assess ambiguous quality criteria, but it substitutes another judgment for the available vendor-master validation and still leaves posting to the model.

sourceNote: What are agents?; Workflow: Prompt chaining — predefined paths and programmatic gates

stem: A support service handles routine account questions and complex troubleshooting. Evaluations show that a lightweight model meets the routine quality target, a larger model is needed for troubleshooting, and an inexpensive intake classifier reliably distinguishes the two. The team wants to reduce routine-query cost without making those users wait for a larger-model call. Which design should it deploy?

options.text: Generate a lightweight-model answer first, then have the larger model assess whether escalation is needed before releasing each response.
Send each inquiry to both models concurrently and have a selector choose the better response once both candidates have completed.
Classify each inquiry at intake and dispatch it to the validated model and prompt for that category, escalating uncertain classifications.
Send each inquiry to the larger model with category-specific prompts, keeping routing inside that call to avoid a separate intake step.

explanation: Routing is appropriate when distinct categories benefit from specialized treatment and classification is accurate. The measured classifier and model evaluations establish those conditions here. Routing routine inquiries directly to their validated lightweight path avoids a larger-model invocation on that path; the alternative designs retain one.

distractorNotes.a: A cascade can be useful when escalation is hard to predict up front, but this version requires a larger-model assessment even for routine questions.
distractorNotes.b: Parallel candidates support comparison, but invoking both models for each inquiry keeps the larger-model cost and waits for its result.
distractorNotes.d: A single larger-model call simplifies dispatch but does not exploit the demonstrated lower-cost routine path.

sourceNote: Workflow: Routing — accurate classification and model specialization

stem: A pull-request review service must check security, architectural conventions, and test coverage. Each focused reviewer meets its quality target without seeing the others' findings; a combined prompt misses issues. Load tests put each focused call below 20 seconds, but the serial chain exceeds the 30-second CI budget. With a budget of three review calls per pull request, which design should the team validate next?

options.text: Run the three focused reviewers concurrently on the pull request and aggregate their findings in code after the calls complete.
Run three general-purpose reviewers concurrently on the pull request and retain findings that appear in a majority of their reports.
Use one call to select the riskiest review dimension and spend the two remaining calls investigating that dimension in more detail.
Keep the focused reviewers in a chain, passing each review's findings forward so later reviewers can avoid reporting duplicates.

explanation: Sectioning runs independent subtasks in parallel and aggregates their outputs. It preserves the three validated specialist checks while removing their unnecessary serial dependency. The scenario's measurements justify testing this architecture against the CI budget; parallelism itself is not a vendor guarantee of a 30-second completion time.

distractorNotes.b: Voting repeats the same task to obtain multiple perspectives. It replaces the validated focused checks with general reviews and can discard a real finding reported by a single reviewer.
distractorNotes.c: Adaptive prioritization can save work, but spending the remaining budget on one dimension leaves required dimensions unchecked.
distractorNotes.d: Sharing prior findings may help deduplication, but the checks do not need that dependency and the measured serial design already exceeds the budget.

sourceNote: Workflow: Parallelization — sectioning versus voting

stem: A repository migration can touch an API client, its callers, generated bindings, and tests in different combinations. Repository analysis is needed to discover the affected components. The team wants specialist workers to make changes concurrently where safe, while one component owns the migration plan and reconciles their results. Which design best satisfies those requirements?

options.text: Partition each repository by directory up front, run the same migration worker on each partition, and concatenate the resulting change reports.
Run several complete migration attempts independently, evaluate each finished patch, and select the attempt with the best test results.
Use a single adaptive coding agent to explore the repository and perform each required edit itself, retaining the investigation in one session.
Have an orchestrator discover affected components, delegate scoped edits with dependencies made explicit, and reconcile the workers' results.

explanation: Orchestrator-workers dynamically decomposes an input, delegates work, and synthesizes results. Unlike fixed sectioning, the subtasks can depend on the repository analysis. That supports the requested central ownership and specialist execution; dependencies still need coordination rather than assuming that every edit can run concurrently.

distractorNotes.a: Static partitions are useful for independent work, but directory boundaries are not the discovered migration boundaries and concatenation does not reconcile cross-component changes.
distractorNotes.b: Independent attempts plus evaluation can select a promising patch, but duplicate the entire migration instead of coordinating complementary specialist work.
distractorNotes.c: A single adaptive agent can discover the edits, but this design does not provide the requested concurrent specialist execution.

sourceNote: Workflow: Orchestrator-workers — input-dependent decomposition and synthesis

stem: A legal drafting service produces usable clauses but often misses corporate style requirements that depend on the deal. Tests show that a model can identify those defects against the firm's rubric, and targeted revisions improve the same draft. The service must preserve already approved wording while resolving the outstanding defects, stopping or escalating after a bounded number of attempts. Which workflow fits best?

options.text: Alternate rubric-based evaluation and targeted revision of the current draft, retaining approved wording and stopping at acceptance or the attempt limit.
Generate independent complete drafts in parallel and use agreement among their phrasings to select the clause most representative of the candidates.
Classify each deal into a contract category and produce a fresh draft from that category's template whenever the reviewer finds a style defect.
Split the rubric among specialist writers, let each independently rewrite the whole clause, and select one finished rewrite for legal review.

explanation: Evaluator-optimizer fits when evaluation criteria are clear, the evaluator can provide useful feedback, and iterative refinement measurably improves outputs. The current draft and its targeted feedback remain the basis of revision here. The attempt limit bounds the process; it does not guarantee that a draft will satisfy the rubric.

distractorNotes.b: Agreement among independent drafts is not a check against the corporate rubric and does not preserve approved wording from the current draft.
distractorNotes.c: Routing can select a useful starting template, but generating a fresh draft on each failure does not use the demonstrated targeted-revision mechanism.
distractorNotes.d: Specialists can examine different rubric dimensions, but independent whole-clause rewrites do not reconcile their feedback into the existing approved draft.

sourceNote: Workflow: Evaluator-optimizer; Agents — evaluation criteria, measurable refinement, stopping conditions

stem: An operations agent restarts services and closes resolved incidents. Its API wrapper logs execution errors for operators but returns the requested action's description to Claude. After a restart fails, Claude sometimes closes the incident as resolved. The team wants the agent to recover from actual failures without repeating successful remediation steps. Which change addresses the faulty feedback loop?

options.text: Add a second model that reviews the planned remediation and the action descriptions before allowing the first model to close the incident.
Have the wrapper retry a failed action several times and return the original action description once its retry policy has finished.
Return the operation's observed outcome and error details to Claude, and use a subsequent health check as evidence before closing the incident.
Restart the agent from the original incident description after a wrapper error, retaining the detailed execution logs in the operator dashboard.

explanation: Anthropic emphasizes ground truth from tool results or code execution at each step so an agent can assess progress. An action description states intent, not outcome. Returning the actual failure and then checking service health gives this agent evidence on which to adapt or escalate without discarding completed work.

distractorNotes.a: A reviewer sees the same intent-only evidence and cannot determine from it whether the restart succeeded.
distractorNotes.b: Bounded retries may recover transient failures, but returning intent after retries still hides an unresolved failure from the agent.
distractorNotes.d: Restarting can help a failed session, but withholding the execution evidence from the new session loses the information needed to avoid repeating completed actions.

sourceNote: Agents — environmental ground truth, tool results, and checkpoints

stem: A research coordinator must preserve the user's detailed assumptions while several independent investigations read long filings and database results. Most raw investigation output is irrelevant after the findings are extracted. The team wants to keep those raw outputs out of the coordinator's conversation rather than repeatedly summarizing its user discussion. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Keep investigation in the coordinator and compact its full conversation after each source, retaining the latest summary as the next turn's context.
Delegate each investigation to a focused subagent with its own context and return findings with source references to the coordinator.
Keep investigation in the coordinator and cache its growing prompt prefix, so repeated user assumptions and source text are reused across calls.
Store progress notes outside the coordinator and reload them after a context reset, keeping the raw investigation calls in its conversation until then.

explanation: Sub-agent architectures separate detailed exploration from high-level synthesis: workers use clean contexts and return distilled findings. Compaction and persistent notes are also valid context-management techniques, but they do not keep the raw investigation traffic out of the coordinator as requested. Prompt caching changes reuse cost and processing time, not which text occupies the context.

distractorNotes.a: Compaction supports long conversations, but applies lossy summarization to the user discussion the scenario specifically wants to preserve.
distractorNotes.c: Prompt caching reuses prefixes; it does not remove the filings and database output from the coordinator's context.
distractorNotes.d: Notes help recover progress across context resets, but this design still puts each investigation's raw output in the coordinator first.

sourceNote: Context engineering for long-horizon tasks — Compaction, Structured note-taking, Sub-agent architectures

stem: An insurer must summarize 100,000 transcripts released at 11 PM before a 7 AM reporting cutoff. Missing reports are not acceptable. A capacity-tested standard Messages API queue can finish with retry headroom under the contracted limits, but a cheaper Message Batches prototype usually finishes much earlier. Which production decision respects the deadline without treating typical batch timing as a guarantee?

options.text: Use the capacity-tested standard queue with deadline monitoring and retry headroom; keep the batch discount out of the deadline commitment.
Submit several smaller Message Batches at 11 PM and use the prototype's observed turnaround as the production completion commitment.
Submit one Message Batch at 11 PM and poll frequently, treating a completed batch status as confirmation that each transcript has a summary.
Submit a Message Batch at 11 PM and resubmit expired requests when its processing window ends, using the retry to complete the morning report.

explanation: The documented batch window is not an eight-hour completion guarantee. Results become available when processing ends or after 24 hours, and requests can expire without being processed. The scenario supplies a capacity-tested standard path with retry headroom, so that is the defensible basis for the deadline. It still needs operational monitoring; neither API choice alone guarantees success.

distractorNotes.b: Smaller batches can help scheduling, but the documentation gives them no shorter guaranteed processing window; prototype timing is not a commitment.
distractorNotes.c: Polling observes progress rather than accelerating it. An ended batch can include errored, canceled, or expired requests, not just successful summaries.
distractorNotes.d: Expiry-based recovery is appropriate for delay-tolerant work, but the documented expiration can occur after the morning deadline.

sourceNote: Batch limitations; Retrieving batch results — 24-hour expiration and per-request result types

stem: An internal HR assistant answers questions from a maintained policy corpus. A retrieval-augmented single-call prototype meets the agreed accuracy and latency targets on representative questions. The next release adds more users but no new actions or multi-step research requirements. The team wants a maintainable production architecture and evidence before accepting extra inference cost. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Add an evaluator-optimizer loop to each answer before rollout, using a second model to review the retrieved evidence and request revisions.
Keep the validated retrieval-plus-generation path, monitor its failure modes, and add orchestration if evaluations establish a need.
Introduce a planning agent that decides which policy sources to search for each question and hands the collected evidence to a writing agent.
Deploy several independent answer generators and a voting stage so that each policy answer is selected from multiple candidate responses.

explanation: Anthropic recommends the simplest solution that works and increasing complexity when it demonstrably improves outcomes. Single LLM calls augmented with retrieval and examples can be sufficient. The tested path already meets this release's requirements, so increased user volume alone does not establish a need for additional model orchestration.

distractorNotes.a: Evaluation and revision can improve outputs when feedback has demonstrated value, but no such gap has been established for this release.
distractorNotes.c: Adaptive research is useful when source selection requires multi-step exploration; that capability is not a requirement of the validated corpus search.
distractorNotes.d: Multiple attempts can improve confidence on some tasks, but they add inference work before a measured quality need has justified it.

sourceNote: When (and when not) to use agents; Combining and customizing these patterns

stem: A database operations agent confuses similarly named cluster tools and repeatedly submits an invalid region identifier after a tool rejects it. The team wants to improve selection and recovery without adding another model call before each operation. Which TWO changes address the observed failures? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Preserve the brief tool specifications and add a planning-model call that selects the cluster operation and formats its arguments before execution.
Clarify the tools' distinct purposes, parameter meanings, and valid input examples in the definitions supplied to the agent.
Expose the same operations through one generic command tool, moving the operation and region conventions into a separate reference manual.
Return an actionable validation error identifying the rejected argument and explaining how to supply a valid region.
Have the wrapper retry rejected requests unchanged and keep the detailed validation diagnostics in operator logs rather than model-visible results.

explanation: Anthropic recommends explicit tool descriptions, unambiguous input parameters, and error responses that explain actionable improvements. Distinct descriptions address selection confusion, while a meaningful validation response gives the agent information needed to repair the region argument. Both improve the existing tool interface rather than adding a planning stage.

distractorNotes.a: A separate planning call can help some workflows, but violates the stated call constraint and leaves the ambiguous interface unchanged.
distractorNotes.c: Consolidation can be useful for coherent workflows, but a generic command plus detached conventions moves the ambiguity into the arguments rather than explaining it.
distractorNotes.e: Retries can recover transient execution failures. An invalid region requires changed input, and operator-only diagnostics do not help the agent make that change.

sourceNote: Optimizing tool responses for token efficiency; Prompt-engineering your tool descriptions

stem: An operations agent may investigate unfamiliar incidents, but repeated unsuccessful diagnostics have kept it running indefinitely. Routine read-only work should remain autonomous; production-changing actions require the on-call engineer's approval, after which the agent should continue without restarting the investigation. Which TWO controls satisfy those requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enforce a maximum iteration count in the runner and return the unresolved investigation for escalation when the limit is reached.
Limit tool requests per minute and use exponential backoff during failures, leaving the agent to decide when its investigation is complete.
Pause at a runner-enforced approval checkpoint before production-changing tools execute, allowing read-only diagnostics to continue autonomously.
Give the agent read-only tools and automatically end its run whenever it proposes a change, requiring an engineer to restart the investigation.
Have a second model review proposed changes against the incident runbook and execute those it judges appropriate without an engineer checkpoint.

explanation: Anthropic describes maximum-iteration stopping conditions for control and human-feedback checkpoints during agent execution. A runner-enforced limit bounds the investigation even if the model keeps requesting diagnostics. A separate approval checkpoint meets this organization's requirement for human authorization without removing autonomous read-only work.

distractorNotes.b: Rate limiting and backoff control request frequency, not the total length of an investigation that continues indefinitely.
distractorNotes.d: Removing write capabilities prevents an unapproved change, but ending and restarting the investigation does not provide the requested approval-and-continue path.
distractorNotes.e: Model review can supplement oversight, but its judgment is not the on-call engineer's approval required by this scenario.

sourceNote: Agents — maximum-iteration stopping conditions and human-feedback checkpoints

stem: An intake service receives narrative-only, table-only, and mixed insurance claims. Validated specialist paths classify narrative intent and extract table fields for arithmetic checks in code. The input parser already identifies which sections are present. Mixed claims need both results, but neither analysis depends on the other. Which composition avoids unnecessary work and serial waiting while retaining the validated paths?

options.text: Dispatch the sections that are present to their specialist paths, run both paths concurrently for mixed claims, and merge their results in code.
Route each claim to one specialist based on its dominant content type, asking that specialist to include the secondary content in its analysis.
Run both specialist paths on each incoming claim and have each return an empty result when the content it handles is absent from the input.
Process narrative content before table content for mixed claims, passing the narrative result into table extraction as additional context.

explanation: Routing selects relevant paths, while sectioning runs independent subtasks concurrently. Anthropic explicitly permits combining patterns to fit the use case. Here the existing parser supplies dispatch information, so an additional model classifier is unnecessary. This composition avoids a serial dependency without claiming a specific latency SLA from the pattern alone.

distractorNotes.b: Routing to one specialist fits mutually exclusive categories, but mixed claims require both independently validated analyses.
distractorNotes.c: Parallel execution avoids serial waiting, but invokes an unnecessary path for each single-content claim despite the parser already identifying the available sections.
distractorNotes.d: Chaining is useful when a later step needs an earlier result. Here it adds a dependency the analyses do not have.

sourceNote: Workflow: Routing; Workflow: Parallelization; Combining and customizing these patterns

stem: A code-security team finds that different review prompts catch different genuine vulnerabilities. It can afford several reviews of the same patch. A candidate reported by one reviewer must remain available for triage, while creating an emergency blocker should require stronger corroboration. Which architecture supports both goals?

options.text: Partition the patch among reviewers, give each a disjoint set of files, and merge their reports before deciding which findings should block release.
Review the same patch with diverse prompts, retain the union of candidate findings, and apply a separate corroboration threshold for emergency blockers.
Review the same patch with diverse prompts, discard findings below the blocker quorum, and use the remaining set for both triage and release decisions.
Chain the review prompts, asking each reviewer to refine the previous report into a replacement report that becomes the input to the next reviewer.

explanation: Parallel voting obtains diverse outputs on the same task; Anthropic describes vulnerability reviews and thresholds that balance false positives and negatives. Retaining candidates separately from the blocker threshold meets the two different requirements. A higher quorum can suppress real minority findings, so consensus must not be described as simultaneously maximizing recall and eliminating false positives.

distractorNotes.a: Sectioning covers different parts of the patch but does not obtain multiple perspectives on the same code for corroboration.
distractorNotes.c: A quorum can be appropriate for disruptive blocker decisions, but using it to discard triage candidates violates the minority-finding requirement.
distractorNotes.d: Successive refinement can improve a report, but replacing the candidate set at each stage does not preserve each reviewer's independent findings for triage.

sourceNote: Workflow: Parallelization — voting, vulnerability review, and false-positive/false-negative thresholds

stem: A procurement assistant must combine contract analysis, inventory findings, and purchasing policy into one recommendation. Specialists need lengthy, largely independent investigations. The integration component should see their conclusions and supporting references, not their search transcripts, and should own the final synthesis. Which architecture best preserves that boundary?

options.text: Use a chain of specialist prompts in one conversation, retaining each investigation's tool output so the final specialist can write the recommendation.
Have peers investigate independently and exchange their full working transcripts, then ask the last available peer to assemble the recommendation.
Have a lead agent delegate focused investigations into separate contexts and synthesize returned findings and references into the recommendation.
Keep one investigating agent, periodically compact its transcript, and use its compacted working history as the basis for the final recommendation.

explanation: The documented sub-agent architecture separates detailed investigation from synthesis: focused workers use clean context windows and return distilled summaries to a lead agent. That directly matches the requested information boundary. Central coordination alone does not make model decisions deterministic or guarantee bounded execution; those are separate control requirements.

distractorNotes.a: A shared chain gives the final specialist the preceding raw tool outputs, contrary to the requested separation.
distractorNotes.b: Peer communication can support collaboration, but circulating full transcripts crosses the information boundary and does not give synthesis to a designated lead.
distractorNotes.d: Compaction helps a long-running single agent, but summarizes investigation inside the same context rather than keeping specialist working contexts separate.

sourceNote: Context engineering for long-horizon tasks — Sub-agent architectures versus Compaction

stem: A SQL-generation service produces plausible queries that sometimes reference missing columns or fail in the target database dialect. A read-only test environment with the target schema is available. Before presenting a query, the team needs evidence about its behavior in that environment and actionable feedback for repair, not just agreement that the SQL looks reasonable. Which design best fits?

options.text: Have a second model review each query against schema documentation and return a correctness score with suggested textual improvements.
Generate several candidate queries independently and present the query whose structure most closely matches the other candidates.
Retrieve a previously approved query for a similar question, then ask Claude to adapt its columns and joins to the current request.
Validate and test the query in the read-only target environment, returning concrete failures to Claude for bounded repair attempts.

explanation: Anthropic recommends grounding agent progress in environmental feedback and describes coding agents iterating using automated test results. Applied here, the supplied database test environment can expose the missing-column and dialect failures directly. Passing those checks is evidence for the tested behavior, not proof that the query answers the business question correctly.

distractorNotes.a: A model reviewer can assess intent or style but does not execute against the target schema and therefore does not supply the requested environmental evidence.
distractorNotes.b: Agreement across plausible queries does not establish that referenced columns exist or that the target database accepts the syntax.
distractorNotes.c: Retrieval supplies a useful starting pattern, but adaptation can introduce the same schema or dialect errors and still needs testing.

sourceNote: Agents — environmental ground truth; Appendix 1 B: Coding agents — automated tests as feedback

stem: A modernization project is converting 200 stored procedures into services. Some procedures share transaction boundaries and temporary tables; others are independent. A prototype assigning one worker per procedure produced incompatible service contracts. The team still wants parallel specialist work but needs cross-procedure decisions settled before implementation. Which decomposition should it use?

options.text: Have a coordinator analyze shared dependencies and settle contracts, then delegate compatible work units and integrate their results against that plan.
Keep one worker per procedure, give each the full procedure catalog, and have each infer the service contracts it needs before producing its implementation.
Divide the procedures into equal-sized worker assignments by name and reconcile incompatible service contracts after the implementations are complete.
Run several independent end-to-end modernization plans with their own implementations and choose the result with the fewest integration failures.

explanation: Orchestrator-workers supports input-dependent decomposition, delegation, and synthesis. Here dependency analysis determines useful work units rather than procedure count alone. Settling shared contracts before delegation addresses the prototype's failure while retaining parallel work where appropriate. The post does not prescribe a global DAG or a specific migration algorithm; those would be additional implementation choices.

distractorNotes.b: Giving each worker more information does not give shared contract decisions a single owner; independently inferred interfaces can remain incompatible.
distractorNotes.c: Equal-sized partitions balance counts but do not respect transaction and shared-table dependencies, postponing the required decisions until after implementation.
distractorNotes.d: Whole-system independent attempts can provide alternatives, but duplicate the full implementation instead of coordinating complementary specialist work under agreed contracts.

sourceNote: Workflow: Orchestrator-workers — dynamic decomposition, delegation, and synthesis

stem: An architect is designing an enterprise legal discovery agent on the Claude Agent SDK that analyzes thousands of litigation documents over an 8-hour execution window. The agent runs on spot cloud compute instances that may terminate with short notice, and a replacement worker starts in a fresh container. If an instance shuts down, the agent must resume without re-processing previously completed documents or re-incurring hundreds of dollars in API token costs. Which state management pattern should the architect implement?

options.text: Rely on the SDK's default session files written to local disk, having the replacement worker pick up the most recent session with the continue option.
Mirror session transcripts to a shared backend through a session-store adapter, and checkpoint per-document completion outside the instance for the replacement host.
Maintain cumulative document progress in a multi-turn conversation thread using prompt caching, relying on cache lifetime to preserve state across instance restarts.
Accumulate document analyses in the container's local scratch storage and batch-upload the completed archive to durable cloud storage at the end of the 8-hour window.

explanation: The Agent SDK documentation states that session files are local to their originating machine and describes session-store adapters that mirror transcripts to a backend another host can access. Resume through the adapter uses a working directory matching the original run because that directory determines the store lookup key. Separately, durable application checkpoints track completed documents and their results; they need not share the transcript backend. This avoids restarting the completed corpus, but does not guarantee recovery of an in-flight operation that had not yet been durably recorded when the instance stopped.

distractorNotes.a: Session files are local to the machine that created them, so continue on a fresh container finds no session to resume. The documentation routes cross-host resume to a session store or to relocating the session file.
distractorNotes.c: Prompt caching accelerates a repeated prefix within its cache lifetime, measured in minutes rather than hours. It is a cost and latency optimization, not a durable record of which documents are done.
distractorNotes.d: Deferring persistence to the end of an 8-hour window means preemption at hour 7 destroys every intermediate result and wastes the accumulated token spend.

sourceNote: Resume across hosts: session files are local to their machine; a session-store adapter mirrors transcripts so another host can resume.

stem: An HR assistant answers staffing questions by resolving an employee, reading their team, and retrieving that team's current assignment. Each step needs an identifier returned by the previous step. Traces show the same sequence on most questions. Existing authorization must remain in force, and answers need live data rather than a periodic snapshot. Which tool redesign best reduces model round trips?

options.text: Keep the three tools and ask Claude to issue their calls concurrently, using employee names in place of identifiers until prior results arrive.
Keep the three tools and improve their descriptions with a worked example of the sequence, so Claude can plan the required calls more reliably.
Expose a staffing-context tool that performs the linked lookups behind the existing authorization checks and returns the relevant combined result.
Build a cached directory of employees, teams, and assignments and include each employee's joined record in the prompt instead of using live tools.

explanation: Anthropic recommends tools that target high-impact workflows and consolidate frequently chained operations behind a coherent interface. Its customer-context example combines related lookups in one tool. The application still performs the necessary authorized data access, but the model no longer needs a separate round trip for each intermediate identifier.

distractorNotes.a: Parallel tool calls fit independent operations. These calls require earlier results, and substituting names does not satisfy the existing identifier contracts.
distractorNotes.b: Better descriptions can improve selection and arguments, but leave the three data dependencies and associated model round trips in place.
distractorNotes.d: A joined snapshot can avoid lookups, but it changes freshness semantics and fails the stated requirement for live data.

sourceNote: Choosing the right tools for agents — consolidate chained operations and return relevant customer context

stem: A diagnostic assistant repeatedly sends the same large troubleshooting manual, then a changing customer question. Traces show substantial repeated prompt-processing time, and the UI waits for the full answer before displaying it. The validated model and complete manual must be retained. The team wants to improve time to the first visible response and then re-measure its latency target. Which change best addresses both observed delays?

options.text: Move to a faster model and shorten generated explanations, retaining the complete manual and returning each answer when generation finishes.
Retrieve a small subset of manual sections for each question and stream the answer, replacing full-manual context with the retrieved excerpts.
Stream answers from the existing model while placing the changing customer question before the manual and caching at the end of the manual.
Cache the unchanged manual prefix before the customer question and stream the existing model's response incrementally to the UI.

explanation: Prompt caching can reduce repeated processing when the prefix is unchanged. The companion [Streaming messages documentation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/streaming) describes SSE delivery of generated output incrementally, avoiding a wait for the complete answer before display. These address the two measured delays while preserving the model and manual. Cache misses and other latency components remain, so the target must be re-measured rather than promised.

distractorNotes.a: Model selection and output length are real latency levers, but this proposal changes the validated model and still buffers the complete response.
distractorNotes.b: Retrieval can reduce input processing, but discarding manual sections violates the full-context requirement of this scenario.
distractorNotes.c: Streaming addresses buffering, but changing content before the manual changes the cumulative prefix and prevents the intended reuse across customer questions.

sourceNote: How prompt caching works; Structuring your prompt — reusable prefixes before varying content

stem: A bank has two workloads. Checkout fraud checks need a complete decision within two seconds; a fast model meets the quality threshold in testing, but peak-load latency is not yet validated. Historical audit analysis is delay-tolerant, can retry incomplete work, and prioritizes token cost. Which TWO architecture decisions are appropriate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Send checkout checks through small Message Batches and poll aggressively, using typical short batch turnaround as the two-second deadline basis.
Use the validated fast model on the direct Messages path for checkout, then load-test end-to-end latency and define a deadline fallback before release.
Use streaming for checkout and consider the latency requirement met when the first token arrives, even if the completed fraud decision is still pending.
Use Message Batches for historical analysis, respecting request and byte limits and reconciling failed or expired requests before declaring the audit complete.
Use a rate-controlled direct Messages queue for historical analysis to obtain the batch token discount while retaining per-request completion control.

explanation: The batch documentation distinguishes asynchronous, discounted work from requests needing immediate responses and requires handling per-request result types and limits. [Reducing latency, Choose the right model](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-latency#1-choose-the-right-model) treats model choice as one latency factor, not a deadline guarantee. Here the tested fast model is a candidate for the direct checkout path, with load validation still required. Delay-tolerant historical work can instead use batch pricing and explicit recovery.

distractorNotes.a: Neither small batch size nor frequent polling provides a two-second completion commitment; unfinished batch requests can expire after the documented processing window.
distractorNotes.c: Streaming improves first-visible-output responsiveness. This business requirement is a completed fraud decision, so first-token timing is the wrong acceptance metric.
distractorNotes.e: A direct queue can control scheduling, but client-side queuing does not qualify standard Messages calls for the Message Batches pricing discount.

sourceNote: Message Batches API; Batch limitations; Pricing; Retrieving batch results

stem: A Claude Code coordinator delegates independent database and application-log investigations. Workers currently inherit broad tool access, and their verbose final reports refill the coordinator with logs. The team wants worker specialization and a compact synthesis context, while preserving access to evidence if a finding is challenged. Which TWO changes best fit? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Launch both investigations as forks of the coordinator so they inherit its full history and tool definitions, avoiding explicit task-context handoffs.
Define focused non-fork subagents with the task context they need and tool access restricted to their respective diagnostic responsibilities.
Keep the broad worker definitions and prepend a prompt telling each worker to prefer its specialty's tools when deciding what to investigate.
Keep verbose worker return messages and compact the coordinator after each result, using its summary to recover the important investigation evidence.
Ask workers to return findings, uncertainties, and evidence references; keep detailed investigation transcripts outside the coordinator's working context.

explanation: The subagent documentation recommends focused agents, limited tool access, and isolating exploration in separate contexts that return summaries. Non-fork workers can use their own definitions rather than inheriting the coordinator's full history and tools. Concise findings with references preserve the synthesis boundary while allowing targeted evidence follow-up instead of copying raw logs into the coordinator.

distractorNotes.a: Forks inherit the parent's full history and tool definitions. That is useful for shared-context side work, but does not provide the requested fresh, specialized worker configurations.
distractorNotes.c: A preference in a prompt does not restrict available tools and leaves the broad capability set in each worker's context.
distractorNotes.d: Compaction is useful for long conversations, but importing raw reports first defeats the requested boundary and makes evidence recovery depend on what summarization retained.

sourceNote: Manage subagent context; How forks differ from other subagents; Example subagents — focused tasks and limited tools
